blocks.text: **The problem.** A board holds `"X"` and `"O"`. A region is a group of `"O"` cells joined up, down, left or right. A region is **surrounded** if none of its cells is on the edge of the board — then it's walled in by `"X"` on every side. Capture every surrounded region by flipping its cells to `"X"`. Change the board in place.

blocks.alt: Left: a 4 by 4 board with a three-cell O region in the middle and a single O on the bottom edge. The middle region is coloured red: it is surrounded. The bottom O is green: it touches the edge. Right: after capturing, the middle region has become X and the bottom O remains.

elements.text: red: walled in   green: on the edge
elements.originalText: red: walled in   green: on the edge

blocks.code:
board = [["X","X","X","X"],          [["X","X","X","X"],
         ["X","O","O","X"],     ->     ["X","X","X","X"],
         ["X","X","O","X"],            ["X","X","X","X"],
         ["X","O","X","X"]]            ["X","O","X","X"]]

The bottom "O" is on the edge, so it is not surrounded and stays.

blocks.text: The pattern: start from the border
The question sounds like it's about the trapped regions: *which O regions are walled in?* Answering it directly means walking each region and checking whether any of its cells touches the edge.

Turn it around. The regions that **escape** are exactly the ones that touch the border — so start there. Walk from every `"O"` on the border and mark everything you can reach as safe. Whatever is left unmarked can't reach the edge, so it's surrounded. Many grid questions get simpler this way: when the edge decides the answer, begin at the edge and walk **inwards**.
Walk every `"O"` region you haven't seen yet, collecting its cells and noting whether any of them is on the border. If none is, flip the whole region. The region list doubles as the BFS queue.

**Time O(m · n), space O(m · n).** Each cell joins one region and is looked at once, so it's already linear — but it needs a `seen` grid, a list per region and a flag, and the capture can only happen after the whole region has been walked.

Walk inwards from every border cell and mark each reachable `"O"` as `"S"` (safe). Then sweep the board once: an `"O"` that was never reached is surrounded, so it becomes `"X"`; every `"S"` goes back to `"O"`. The board itself is the visited marker.

blocks.caption: Walk in from the border marking safe cells, then capture whatever is left. Try the board with an escape route.

blocks.text: **Time O(m · n), space O(m · n).** Each `"O"` is marked at most once, and the final sweep reads every cell once. The only extra memory is the recursion, which is as deep as the longest safe region; use a queue instead if the board can be huge.

blocks.alt: Check each region: O(m·n) time, O(m·n) space. From the border: O(m·n) time, O(m·n) space.

blocks.text: Same cost, but the border version needs no `seen` grid, no region lists and no flags — just one mark and one sweep. That simplicity is the point of the pattern, and in the next lesson it also turns a slow answer into a fast one.

items: **A board one or two cells wide** — every cell is on the border, so nothing can be captured.
**An O region that touches the border at one corner cell** — the whole region is safe.
**Diagonal contact** — an inner `"O"` touching a safe one only diagonally is still surrounded.
**No O at all, or all O** — nothing changes either way.
**Number of Enclaves** — count the land cells that can't walk off the grid: mark from the border, then count what's left.
**Number of Closed Islands** — sink every island touching the border first, then count the islands that remain.
**Pacific Atlantic Water Flow** — start from the border twice, once per ocean. Next lesson.
